report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is substantially **true**, with an important qualifier: tenofovir is an *adjunct* to—rather than replacement for—newborn hepatitis-B vaccination (and, where used, hepatitis-B immune globulin).

The strongest direct evidence is a randomized trial of 200 HBeAg-positive mothers with HBV DNA >200,000 IU/mL. Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), begun at 30–32 weeks and continued to postpartum week 4, reduced infant HBV infection at 28 weeks postpartum compared with no maternal antiviral treatment (intention-to-treat: 5% vs 18%; per-protocol: 0% vs 7%). Infants received immunoprophylaxis. This is strong evidence that late-pregnancy TDF reduces residual transmission risk in highly viremic mothers.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1508660

The WHO consequently recommends TDF prophylaxis for HBsAg-positive pregnant women with HBV DNA ≥200,000 IU/mL (5.3 log10 IU/mL), starting from week 28, alongside timely infant vaccination.  
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK561126/

There are limitations behind a categorical reading of the claim. Transmission is already very low when infant prophylaxis is delivered promptly and correctly; therefore the absolute benefit of maternal TDF varies by setting and baseline risk. A 2023 Cochrane review also judged several infant and safety outcomes uncertain, reflecting limited trial data, heterogeneous regimens, and uncommon transmission events—not evidence that TDF is ineffective.  
https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD013653.pub2/full

Thus, “reduces transmission” is supported for the specified high-viral-load group; it should not be generalized to all pregnant people with chronic HBV or used instead of neonatal immunization.
